summary: This document defines the multipart/multilingual MIME content type. It lets one email message contain several language versions of the same information, each identified by a language tag, so the recipient's software can show the version that suits them best.

eli5.summary: It is like a letter that has the same message written in several languages, and the reader's mailbox picks the one you understand.

questions: how to send an email in multiple languages
how does email choose a language part
what is the zxx language tag
subtitle: A MIME type that packs several language versions of one email into a single message.

tldr.problem: Email has stayed a single-language tool, while teams and companies span many languages and need to reach everyone without miscommunication.
tldr.mechanism: The multipart/multilingual MIME type holds a preface, one language part per translation and an optional language-independent part. Each language part carries a Content-Language tag, and the email client shows the best match for the reader.
tldr.outcome: One message can serve readers of many languages. Clients that do not understand the type treat it as multipart/mixed, so the preface explains the layout.

today: RFC 8255 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC.

sections.title: Why a Multilingual Message Type
sections.content:
Email has remained a single-language tool, even though many organizations span continents, cultures and languages. multipart/multilingual is an addition to the Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions (MIME) standard that lets a sender address a group so that every recipient can read the email in a preferred language.

The way the translations are produced is out of scope. The RFC defines only the structure of the message.
sections.eli5: People who speak different languages often work together. This lets one email carry a version for each of them.

sections.title: The Parts of a Multilingual Message
sections.content:
The Content-Type looks like Content-Type: multipart/multilingual; boundary=01189998819991197253. It has similar semantics to multipart/alternative: every part is another version of the same information. The difference is that the part to render is chosen by the Content-Language field, and optionally Content-Translation-Type, instead of by part order and content types.

A message has exactly one multilingual preface, one or more language message parts, and zero or one language-independent part. The preface SHOULD be present, MUST come first, MUST NOT carry a Content-Language field, SHOULD be text/plain and SHOULD explain the layout in the languages provided. Language parts MUST have Content-Language and Content-Type, SHOULD be message/rfc822 (or MAY be message/global) and should carry a Subject in their own language. The optional last part, with Content-Language zxx, could hold language-independent graphics.
sections.eli5: The envelope has a cover note, then one page per language, and maybe a picture page that anyone can understand.

sections.title: Choosing Which Part to Show
sections.content:
A client that does not understand the type treats the message as multipart/mixed, so the reader sees the preface and the parts in sequence or as attachments. A conforming client SHOULD ignore the preface and select the best match for the user's preferred language from the language parts. The matching schemes in RFC 4647 are RECOMMENDED as a starting point.

If nothing matches, or no language preference is known, the client SHOULD pick the language-independent part if one exists, otherwise the first language part after the preface. Senders therefore SHOULD put the language most likely to be recognized first. The Subject shown SHOULD come from the selected part, falling back to the top-level Subject. Interactive clients MAY let the user pick a language or see them all.
sections.eli5: Your mailbox reads the labels on each page and picks the one that matches your language. If none match, it shows the first page, or the picture page if there is one.

sections.title: Language and Translation Type Fields
sections.content:
Content-Language names the language of a part. It MUST comply with RFC 3282 and BCP 47 (RFC 5646). Examples are en-GB, de, es-MX, fr and sr-Cyrl.

Content-Translation-Type says how a part was produced. The values are original, human (translated or corrected by a person) and automated (translated by an electronic agent with no proofreading). Other values may be added later. A user may prefer an original in their second language over a machine translation in their first, and this field supports that choice. If no preference is known, the field may be ignored.
sections.eli5: Each page has a sticker for its language and another saying whether it is the original, hand-translated or machine-translated.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content: The RFC gives three examples from a sender to a recipient. The first has a preface and two language parts, English (en-GB, original) and Spanish (es, human). The second adds a language-independent PNG image with Content-Language: zxx. The third makes each language part a multipart/alternative of plain text and HTML, so a client needs further processing to choose what to display.
sections.eli5: The examples show a letter with two languages, then the same letter with a picture, then a fancier one where each page has a plain and a decorated copy.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: The RFC registers the multipart/multilingual media type, which requires the boundary parameter defined in RFC 2046. It also adds Content-Translation-Type to the "Permanent Message Header Field Names" registry, and creates a new registry, "Content-Translation-Type Header Field Values", with original, human and automated as initial entries. New values use the Specification Required procedure.
sections.eli5: The official list of email types and labels got new entries so everyone uses the same names.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Language parts are meant to be direct translations, but they may not be. Undesirable text or images could slip past a spam filter that does not check every part, although an unknown multipart subtype should be treated as multipart/mixed so each part is scanned. A recipient might also forward content they cannot read, assuming it matches the part they can; an interactive client can mitigate this by showing all translations for comparison.

Because parts are message/rfc822 or message/global, they may carry From fields that differ from the top-level From and could mislead the reader in a non-conforming client. Each part's From MUST include the same email address as the top-level one, and the top-level value SHOULD be shown on mismatch.
sections.eli5: Someone could hide something odd on a page in a language you cannot read. So mail programs should check every page, and you can look at all the versions if you are unsure.

children.label: Language message part
children.note: one or more, message/rfc822, Content-Language required

children.label: Language-independent part
children.note: zero or one, last, Content-Language zxx

items.label: Original
items.desc: The part is in the original language.

items.label: Human
items.desc: Translated by a person, or an automated translation checked and corrected by a person.

items.label: Automated
items.desc: Translated by an electronic agent without proofreading or correction.
